extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, factors, and procedural rules the PTAB applies when deciding whether to institute an inter partes review and how to evaluate patentability/contentions (claim construction, POSITA, obviousness). Useful for practitioners preparing or opposing IPR petitions and for judges/administrative personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for institution under 35 U.S.C. § 314
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 314 provides that an inter partes review may not be instituted unless the information presented in the Petition “shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision to institute under § 314 may not institute on fewer than all claims challenged in the petition (SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu). Per Board practice, if the Board institutes trial, it will institute on all of the challenged claims and on all grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)). The institution decision assesses whether petitioner has demonstrated a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim based on the petition and preliminary record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for discretionary denial based on parallel district court litigation (Fintiv factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: When exercising discretion under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) in view of parallel district court proceedings, the Board considers factors to assess whether efficiency, fairness, and the merits support denial: (1) whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that one may be granted; (2) proximity of the court’s trial date to the Board’s projected statutory deadline for a final written decision; (3) investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and the parties; (4) overlap between issues raised in the petition and in the parallel proceeding; (5) whether the petitioner and the defendant in the parallel proceeding are the same party; and (6) other circumstances that impact the Board’s exercise of discretion, including the merits (Apple Inc. v. Fintiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board takes a holistic view of these factors (efficiency and integrity). Each factor can weigh for or against discretionary denial; the Board considers them together rather than mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s Guidance on applying Fintiv (Interim Procedure clarifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director’s June 21, 2022 Guidance Memo clarifies application of the Fintiv factors: the precedential import of Fintiv is limited to its facts; the PTAB will not rely on Fintiv factors to deny institution where a petition presents compelling evidence of unpatentability; and the PTAB will consider median district-court time-to-trial statistics when assessing proximity of trial dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Compelling, meritorious challenges” are those in which the evidence, if unrebutted in trial, would plainly lead to a conclusion that one or more claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence. The Guidance Memo also states the PTAB will not discretionarily deny institution where a petitioner presents a stipulation not to pursue in the parallel proceeding the same grounds or any grounds that could have reasonably been raised before the PTAB (consistent with Sotera Wireless). When considering proximity of trial dates, the PTAB will consider median time from filing to disposition for the district where the parallel litigation resides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner’s initial burden and particularity requirement (§ 312(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. (Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim. This is a continuing burden on the petitioner at institution stage and throughout trial; failure to identify particularized evidence can defeat institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion remains with the petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of persuasion never shifts to Patent Owner in an IPR proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the petitioner presents substantial evidence, Patent Owner is not required to carry the burden of persuasion; petitioner must establish unpatentability by the required standard (preponderance) for institution and at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis framework (Graham factors and KSR principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is resolved based on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (Graham). The inquiry typically requires articulation of a reason to combine known elements in the claimed fashion (KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reason to combine may be found in market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings, need or problem known in the field, and the background knowledge/creativity/common sense of a POSITA. The petitioner cannot rely on mere conclusory statements to show obviousness (In re Magnum Oil Tools); must articulate reasoning with some rational underpinning. When in evidence, objective indicia of nonobviousness are considered and may overcome apparent teachings of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in PTAB IPR proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are interpreted using the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b)). Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining meaning, the Board looks principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) is less significant than intrinsic evidence. Any special definition for a claim term must be set forth in the specification with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (In re Paulsen). The Board construes only those terms in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu). Parties are expected to assert claim-construction arguments and evidence in the specified filings (Petition, Patent Owner’s Response, Petitioner’s Reply, Patent Owner’s Sur-reply) and a final determination will be made at the close of the proceeding after hearing and full record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of ordinary skill in the art is typically evidenced by the references themselves; parties may propose a descriptive formulation (e.g., at least a Bachelor’s Degree in electrical engineering, computer science, or computer engineering and at least two years relevant experience), with graduate education or significant work experience substituting for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party proffers a POSITA definition consistent with the subject matter and references, the Board will apply that description for decision purposes. Case law (Okajima, In re GPAC, In re Oelrich) supports using the references as evidence for skill level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of extrinsic evidence and dictionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence such as dictionaries may be cited to support a proposed claim construction, but extrinsic evidence is less significant than the intrinsic record in determining legally operative meaning of claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners and Patent Owners may cite extrinsic sources (e.g., American Heritage, Merriam-Webster) to support constructions, but the Board will prioritize specification and prosecution history; special definitions must be present in the specification to control over ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of objective evidence of nonobviousness in the obviousness inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: When in evidence, the Board considers any relevant objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) in determining obviousness (Graham).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if prior art teaching would have suggested the claimed invention, the totality of evidence, including objective indicia such as commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results, may lead to a conclusion that the claims would not have been obvious. At institution stage Patent Owner may present such evidence in its Preliminary Response; absence of such evidence is noted in institution analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board practice regarding scope of institution and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board institutes trial, the trial will be authorized on all grounds set forth in the Petition and will be conducted according to a corresponding Scheduling Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The institution Order will state that trial is authorized on all grounds and commence on entry date; scheduling order will govern subsequent deadlines and proceedings. Parties should expect institution to open full trial on all challenged claims and grounds raised in the petition (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).
